title: Adrenal Crisis
clinicalScenario: Outline only. Planned scope: Recognition in known and unknown adrenal insufficiency, immediate steroid and fluid treatment, precipitants, steroid sick-day rules. Candidate sources to verify: Society for Endocrinology adrenal crisis guidance; Endocrine Society primary adrenal insufficiency guideline.

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult (over 18 years) Emergency Department (ED) recognition and emergency treatment of adrenal crisis in people with known or suspected adrenal insufficiency, based on the Worcestershire Acute Hospitals NHS Trust guideline (WAHT-END-017 version 2.1, 2025) and the Society for Endocrinology adrenal crisis information page. Paediatric doses are outside this protocol. No Saudi national guideline was found.
findings: Full protocol rebuilt from the source dossier opened on 2026-10-21; exact source locations are recorded in each investigation and medicine row.
The original outline remains preserved; this additive version is non-current and pending clinical review.
unverifiedSections: Normal ranges are typical adult values, not from the cited sources.
Symptoms, signs, differentials and pathophysiology are standard clinical content and were not extracted line by line.

The hydrocortisone infusion preparation (diluent, volume and rate for 200 mg over 24 hours) and the IV glucose volume are not stated in the opened sources; the glucose row refers to the hypoglycaemia protocol. The Society for Endocrinology page is undated and has no numbered sections; the 2016 Society for Endocrinology emergency guidance could not be opened (PubMed Central captcha, not bypassed).
No Saudi national or Saudi Ministry of Health adrenal crisis guideline was found; Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) availability of hydrocortisone injection and fludrocortisone was not checked.

Renal, hepatic and age adjustments for the drugs added in this revision are from manufacturer labels (UK Summary of Product Characteristics, US prescribing information and a New Zealand data sheet), not from Saudi Food and Drug Authority labels.

pathophysiology.summary: Adrenal crisis is acute cortisol deficiency that cannot meet the body's stress needs, causing shock, low sodium, high potassium and low glucose.
keyMechanisms: It occurs in primary adrenal insufficiency, secondary adrenal insufficiency and after long-term steroids when doses are missed or not increased in illness.
Precipitants in the Worcestershire guideline: other infections 25%, gastrointestinal illness 23%, peri-surgery 10% and physiological stress or pain 9%.
Treatment is immediate hydrocortisone and rapid saline; it must never wait for tests.

symptoms: Abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, weakness, dizziness, confusion, fever.
physicalSigns: Hypotension or shock, dehydration, hypoglycaemia, reduced consciousness; pigmentation in primary disease.
redFlags: Hypotension or shock in a patient on long-term steroids or with known adrenal insufficiency.
Vomiting or diarrhoea in a patient with adrenal insufficiency.
Low sodium, high potassium or low glucose.
Steroid emergency card or hydrocortisone injection kit carried.
precipitants: Infection, gastrointestinal illness, surgery, trauma, pain, missed steroid doses.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Source of infection and raised markers, though adrenal crisis may coexist
Responds to fluids alone without steroid dependence
No steroid history; no electrolyte pattern

clinicalManagement.title: Immediate
actions: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM immediately; never wait for results.
Give 500 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride over 15 minutes through a large cannula.
Check capillary glucose and treat hypoglycaemia with IV glucose.
If the patient is not known to have adrenal insufficiency, take paired cortisol and ACTH before hydrocortisone only if this does not delay treatment.

clinicalManagement.title: Ongoing
actions: If stable and sodium is not low, rehydrate carefully with about 3–4 L over 24 hours.
Continue hydrocortisone as 200 mg over 24 hours (infusion) or 50 mg IV or IM every 6 hours.
Continue fludrocortisone at the same dose if already prescribed.
Monitor blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and glucose; find and treat the precipitant.

clinicalManagement.title: Escalation
actions: Shock not responding to the first 500 mL: senior and critical care review.
Persistent low sodium in primary disease: specialist advice on added sodium chloride.

clinicalManagement.title: Disposition
actions: Admit all adrenal crises; refer to endocrinology.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Suspected adrenal crisis is treated at once without waiting for tests
Low sodium, high potassium, low glucose

values: 200 mg over 24 hours (infusion) or 50 mg IV or IM four times daily; consider 100 mg four times daily if BMI 40 or above
200 mg over 24 hours preferably as continuous infusion, or 50 mg IV or IM every 6 hours
500 mL 0.9% over 15 minutes, then 3–4 L over 24 hours if stable
Rapid rehydration with 0.9% saline; no volume or rate given
Until clinical recovery and endocrinology advice

learningObjectives: Recognise adrenal crisis and give hydrocortisone before tests.
Resuscitate with 500 mL saline over 15 minutes and choose a maintenance regimen.
pitfalls: Delaying hydrocortisone to obtain a cortisol.
Using too little saline or forgetting glucose.
Discharging without a kit, sick day rules or follow-up.
keyPoints: Treat on suspicion; do not wait for tests.
Hydrocortisone 100 mg then 200 mg over 24 hours.
